lessonTitle: Diabetes, Anaemia and Infection in Pregnancy

blocks.text: A 34-year-old woman with a body mass index of 36 and a mother who has type 2 diabetes feels well at 26 weeks. Her fundal height is 3 cm ahead of dates. Nothing in her urine dipstick or blood pressure is abnormal, yet a single two-hour blood test is about to change how her pregnancy is monitored, how she delivers and how her baby is looked after in the first hours of life.

blocks.markdown: Pregnancy places the body under metabolic, haematological and infective stress. Three common problems, **gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM)**, **anaemia** and **infections including malaria and urinary tract infection**, are often silent at first, are found by screening and are largely preventable or treatable. This lesson follows the same order for each: why pregnancy predisposes, how to detect it, how to treat it, and what is at stake for mother and baby.

blocks.title: Gestational diabetes mellitus
blocks.text: Gestational diabetes is glucose intolerance with onset or first recognition in pregnancy. It arises because placental hormones (human placental lactogen, cortisol, progesterone, growth hormone variants) cause insulin resistance, and beta-cell secretion fails to compensate. Fetal hyperinsulinaemia then drives macrosomia.

blocks.markdown: **Screening.** In the UK, NICE recommends a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) at **24 to 28 weeks** for women with risk factors: BMI above 30 kg/m2, a previous baby weighing 4.5 kg or more, previous GDM, a first-degree relative with diabetes, or a family origin with a high prevalence of diabetes. Women with previous GDM are offered early self-monitoring or an OGTT soon after booking and again at 24 to 28 weeks if normal. NICE diagnoses GDM if the **fasting plasma glucose is 5.6 mmol/L or more**, or the **2-hour value is 7.8 mmol/L or more**. Other bodies (WHO, IADPSG) use different cut-offs, and results in mg/dL are converted to mmol/L by dividing by about 18.

blocks.title: Interpreting an OGTT
blocks.prompt: A woman at 27 weeks has a 75 g OGTT. Fasting glucose is 5.2 mmol/L and the 2-hour glucose is 8.4 mmol/L. Does she have GDM by NICE criteria?

steps.text: Compare the fasting value with the NICE threshold.
Compare the 2-hour value with the threshold.
Only one criterion is needed, so the diagnosis is made. Teach self-monitoring and begin a trial of diet and exercise.

blocks.answer: Yes, she has gestational diabetes by NICE criteria because her 2-hour glucose exceeds 7.8 mmol/L, even though her fasting value is normal.

blocks.markdown: **Management of GDM** follows a stepwise plan. First, advice on diet (low glycaemic index carbohydrate) and exercise for one to two weeks. If targets are not met, add **metformin**, and then **insulin** if still not controlled, or from the outset if fasting glucose is 7.0 mmol/L or more. Home capillary targets are commonly fasting below 5.3 mmol/L, 1 hour post meal below 7.8 mmol/L or 2 hours post meal below 6.4 mmol/L. The pregnancy is monitored with serial ultrasound for fetal growth and amniotic fluid, and the woman is generally offered birth by 40+6 weeks. Risks include macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, polyhydramnios, pre-eclampsia, stillbirth and neonatal hypoglycaemia. **After delivery**, hypoglycaemic treatment stops and the woman is tested (fasting glucose or HbA1c) at 6 to 13 weeks and then yearly, because her lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes is high.

rows: Diet, exercise, then metformin or insulin
Oral iron; IV iron if intolerant or late
Preterm birth, low birth weight, postpartum haemorrhage tolerance reduced
Prevention with nets and preventive therapy; urgent treatment
Severe maternal anaemia, placental malaria, low birth weight, stillbirth
blocks.caption: Common medical complications compared.

blocks.markdown: **Anaemia.** In pregnancy plasma volume rises more than red cell mass, so haemoglobin concentration falls physiologically. The British Society for Haematology defines anaemia as haemoglobin below **110 g/L in the first and third trimesters**, below **105 g/L in the second trimester** and below 100 g/L postpartum. **Iron deficiency** is by far the commonest cause, followed by folate deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency and haemoglobinopathies. A low mean cell volume with a low ferritin (often below 30 micrograms per litre) points to iron deficiency; a high MCV suggests folate or B12 deficiency; a low MCV with normal or high ferritin raises thalassaemia or sickle cell trait. Treatment of iron deficiency is oral ferrous salts (for example ferrous sulfate 200 mg, containing 65 mg of elemental iron; a teaching example), taken once daily or on alternate days with a repeat haemoglobin check after about two weeks. **Intravenous iron** is used for oral intolerance, non-response or late presentation near term.

blocks.title: Assessing a low haemoglobin
blocks.prompt: At 32 weeks a woman has haemoglobin 98 g/L, MCV 71 fL and ferritin 9 micrograms per litre. Is she anaemic, what is the likely cause and what is the plan?

steps.text: Compare with the third trimester threshold of 110 g/L.
Interpret the indices: low MCV and a very low ferritin are typical of iron deficiency anaemia, the most common cause.

Plan: start oral iron, counsel on dietary iron and adherence, repeat the full blood count after two weeks and, if the rise is inadequate or she is intolerant, give intravenous iron. Plan for delivery in a unit able to manage haemorrhage.

blocks.answer: She has iron deficiency anaemia and should start oral iron with a repeat haemoglobin in about two weeks.

blocks.markdown: **Malaria** is more frequent and more severe in pregnant women because pregnancy suppresses cell-mediated immunity and *P. falciparum*-infected red cells sequester in the placenta. Consequences include severe maternal anaemia, hypoglycaemia, cerebral malaria, pulmonary oedema, miscarriage, preterm birth, intrauterine growth restriction and stillbirth. In endemic areas WHO recommends **insecticide-treated bed nets**, **intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP)** at each scheduled antenatal visit from the second trimester (at least one month apart), and prompt diagnosis and treatment of fever. Severe malaria needs intravenous artesunate.

**Urinary tract infection.** Progesterone relaxes ureteric smooth muscle, the gravid uterus compresses the ureters and urine stasis occurs, so bacteria ascend more easily. **Asymptomatic bacteriuria** (a significant growth, usually 10 to the fifth colony-forming units per mL or more, on midstream culture) is found in a few percent of women and, if untreated, about a quarter progress to acute **pyelonephritis**, which causes fever, loin pain, preterm labour and sepsis. All women are offered culture at booking, and a positive result is treated with a short, culture-guided antibiotic course chosen to be safe in pregnancy (for example avoiding trimethoprim in the first trimester because it is a folate antagonist). Pyelonephritis requires admission and intravenous antibiotics.

items: GDM: screen at 24 to 28 weeks if at risk, treat with diet then metformin then insulin, and retest after delivery.
Anaemia: use trimester-specific haemoglobin thresholds; replace iron orally, intravenously if needed.
Malaria: bed nets and IPTp-SP in endemic areas; treat promptly.
Bacteriuria: screen and treat, even when asymptomatic.

blocks.title: Know both the cut-off and the reason
blocks.text: Examiners reward the principle: dilutional change explains physiological anaemia, placental sequestration explains malaria in pregnancy, and ureteric stasis explains bacteriuria. Quote cut-offs but note that they vary by guideline.

points: Gestational diabetes is screened with a 75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks in at-risk women and managed with diet, metformin then insulin, followed by postnatal glucose testing.
Anaemia in pregnancy is defined by trimester-specific haemoglobin cut-offs; iron deficiency is most common and is treated with oral or intravenous iron.
Malaria in pregnancy risks severe maternal disease and low birth weight and is prevented by nets and IPTp-SP.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria must be screened for and treated to prevent pyelonephritis and preterm birth.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with a BMI of 33 kg/m2 and no previous diabetes is at booking. When should a 75 g OGTT ordinarily be offered?

distractorRationale.a: Early testing is reserved for women with previous GDM.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: placental insulin resistance peaks later, so risk-factor-positive women are tested at 24 to 28 weeks.
distractorRationale.c: Too late to allow treatment and monitoring.
distractorRationale.d: Dipstick glycosuria is insensitive and non-specific in pregnancy.

questions.explanation: A BMI above 30 kg/m2 is a risk factor for GDM, so she is offered a 75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks. This timing coincides with the rise in placental anti-insulin hormones.

questions.stem: A woman at 25 weeks has a 75 g OGTT: fasting 5.4 mmol/L and 2-hour 8.1 mmol/L. Using NICE criteria, what is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.text: Gestational diabetes because the 2-hour value is at least 7.8 mmol/L
Gestational diabetes because the fasting value is at least 5.6 mmol/L

questions.correctOptionText: Gestational diabetes because the 2-hour value is at least 7.8 mmol/L

distractorRationale.a: The 2-hour value exceeds the diagnostic threshold.
distractorRationale.c: The fasting value of 5.4 is below 5.6 mmol/L.
distractorRationale.d: Nothing in the history indicates type 1 diabetes; hyperglycaemia first found in pregnancy is GDM.

questions.explanation: NICE requires only one abnormal value, and 8.1 mmol/L exceeds the 7.8 mmol/L 2-hour limit. The fasting value of 5.4 is normal, so the diagnosis rests on the 2-hour result.

questions.stem: A woman at 29 weeks has haemoglobin 97 g/L, MCV 72 fL and ferritin 8 micrograms per litre. Haemoglobin electrophoresis is normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral iron, with a repeat haemoglobin in about two weeks
No treatment because anaemia is physiological

questions.correctOptionText: Oral iron, with a repeat haemoglobin in about two weeks

distractorRationale.a: Transfusion is reserved for severe or symptomatic anaemia, or late presentation with decompensation.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: iron deficiency is confirmed by low MCV and ferritin.
distractorRationale.c: Folate is not the deficiency here; the MCV is low, not high.
distractorRationale.d: Haemoglobin is below the second trimester threshold of 105 g/L so it exceeds physiological dilution.

questions.explanation: A low MCV and a very low ferritin with normal electrophoresis indicate iron deficiency, treated with oral iron. A repeat haemoglobin after about two weeks confirms response; intravenous iron is used if there is intolerance or no response.

questions.stem: A primigravida attends her first antenatal visit at 14 weeks in a malaria-endemic region. Which combination best reflects WHO-recommended prevention?

options.text: Insecticide-treated bed net and intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine from the second trimester
Avoid all antenatal visits to reduce exposure

questions.correctOptionText: Insecticide-treated bed net and intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine from the second trimester

distractorRationale.b: Iron treats anaemia but does not prevent malaria.
distractorRationale.c: Antenatal care reduces risk and is where IPTp is delivered.

questions.explanation: Bed nets prevent mosquito bites and IPTp-SP given at scheduled visits from the second trimester at least one month apart clears placental parasitaemia. Together these reduce maternal anaemia and low birth weight.

questions.stem: A midstream urine specimen at booking grows Escherichia coli at 10 to the fifth colony-forming units per mL. The woman has no symptoms. Which statement best justifies treatment?

options.text: Treatment is unnecessary because she has no symptoms
Without treatment a substantial proportion will develop pyelonephritis with a risk of preterm birth
Treatment is only needed after delivery

questions.correctOptionText: Without treatment a substantial proportion will develop pyelonephritis with a risk of preterm birth

distractorRationale.a: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in pregnancy, unlike in most non-pregnant women.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: ureteric dilatation and stasis allow ascending infection.
distractorRationale.c: Urinary infection and GDM are unrelated.
distractorRationale.d: Delay increases the risk of pyelonephritis during pregnancy.

questions.explanation: Pregnancy-related ureteric dilatation and stasis make ascending infection likely, and untreated bacteriuria commonly progresses to pyelonephritis. Pyelonephritis is associated with preterm labour and maternal sepsis, so a short culture-guided antibiotic course is given.

questions.stem: True or false: A woman whose gestational diabetes resolved after delivery needs no further glucose testing.
questions.explanation: Women who have had GDM have a substantially increased lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes, so they are tested at 6 to 13 weeks postnatally (fasting glucose or HbA1c) and then screened yearly. Resolution after delivery does not remove this risk.

questions.stem: A woman is prescribed ferrous fumarate 210 mg tablets (teaching example), each containing 68 mg of elemental iron, to be taken twice daily. How many milligrams of elemental iron does she take per day (answer in mg)?
questions.explanation: Each tablet supplies 68 mg of elemental iron and two tablets are taken, so the daily dose is 68 multiplied by 2, which is 136 mg. The elemental iron, not the salt mass, determines the therapeutic dose.

questions.stem: An American laboratory reports a fasting plasma glucose of 108 mg/dL for a pregnant woman. Using the conversion 1 mmol/L equals 18 mg/dL, calculate the fasting glucose in mmol/L (give to one decimal place).
questions.explanation: Dividing 108 mg/dL by 18 gives 6.0 mmol/L. This exceeds the NICE fasting threshold of 5.6 mmol/L, so it would be diagnostic of gestational diabetes.

questions.stem: A woman at 28 weeks has just been diagnosed with gestational diabetes. Describe her management during the rest of pregnancy and after delivery, and give three risks to the baby.
markingGuide: Education and self-monitoring of capillary glucose with targets (for example fasting below 5.3 mmol/L)
Diet and exercise for one to two weeks as first step
Add metformin if targets are not met, then insulin; insulin immediately if fasting glucose is very high
Serial growth ultrasound and amniotic fluid assessment
Plan for delivery by 40+6 weeks with consideration of mode of birth
After delivery: stop hypoglycaemic treatment, check neonatal glucose, test the mother at 6 to 13 weeks and yearly
Neonatal risks: macrosomia and birth injury, neonatal hypoglycaemia, respiratory distress or stillbirth
questions.explanation: Maternal hyperglycaemia crosses the placenta and drives fetal hyperinsulinaemia, hence macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycaemia once the maternal glucose supply is cut at birth. Postnatal testing is required because of a persistent risk of type 2 diabetes.

questions.stem: Explain why malaria and urinary tract infection are more dangerous in pregnancy, and outline how each is prevented or detected.
markingGuide: Malaria: reduced cell-mediated immunity and placental sequestration of P. falciparum-infected red cells
Malaria complications: severe anaemia, hypoglycaemia, cerebral malaria, miscarriage, preterm birth, low birth weight, stillbirth
Malaria prevention: insecticide-treated nets, IPTp-SP at antenatal visits from the second trimester, prompt diagnosis and treatment
UTI: progesterone-mediated smooth muscle relaxation and uterine compression cause ureteric dilatation and urinary stasis
Asymptomatic bacteriuria progresses to pyelonephritis in a substantial proportion if untreated, with preterm labour risk
UTI detection and prevention: midstream urine culture at booking and culture-guided antibiotics, plus hydration advice
questions.explanation: Both infections exploit physiological adaptations of pregnancy: immune modulation and placental sequestration for malaria, and urinary stasis for UTI. Screening and preventive therapy interrupt the path to maternal and fetal harm.
